events.text:
🇸🇦💧 Saudi Arabia’s Worst Oil Nightmare May Be Just Beginning
Saudi Arabia built a pipeline to get its oil around trouble in the Persian Gulf, but trouble has proved less attached to geography. An October 13 attack on an Aramco administrative building in Dhahran caused a limited fire, according to the Saudi Energy Ministry, bringing the fighting into the kingdom’s oil-rich Eastern Province. No casualties were reported.
After the October 10 Houthi missile strike on King Khalid International Airport killed at least 13 people, Saudi authorities now have another reminder that buying weapons and keeping vital sites safe are different achievements. Repeated attacks have disrupted flights, with the pressure extending from passenger terminals to Aramco’s doorstep.
The East-West Pipeline was supposed to give Saudi oil some breathing room by carrying crude across the country to Yanbu on the Red Sea, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz. Aramco says the route helped sustain production and exports during disruptions in the strait.
Once the oil reaches Yanbu, though, the map presents another awkward detail: tankers heading south must pass through Bab el-Mandeb, where the Houthis threaten shipping. Cargoes can also sail north toward Suez, so claims that Saudi exports are completely trapped go too far. The detour exists; a trouble-free journey is another matter.
Both coasts need oil from functioning production and processing facilities in eastern Saudi Arabia. Changing the departure port does little good if those facilities are damaged. The Dhahran fire does not establish a production outage, but it gives Saudi planners another reason to look beyond the shipping lanes.
An even worse scenario would be Iran encouraging unrest and sabotage in the oil-rich Eastern Province, with attacks on foreign specialists potentially driving skilled workers out. Saudi Arabia could then struggle to keep its oil facilities running even if its export routes stayed open.
Saudi Arabia already has to protect airports, oil facilities and export routes at once, while the Houthis can choose where to strike. They do not have to defeat the Saudi military to disrupt the economy it protects. An alternative export route is useful insurance, but the policy does not cover everything.

🗣The underground network keeping Houthis in the fight
From 2015-2022, the Saudi-led coalition conducted 25k+ air raids over Yemen, with hundreds more carried out since the July 2026 escalation.
Saudi Arabia possesses 900+ military aircraft, including 150+ F-15 and 72 Eurofighter Typhoon jets, plus AWACS, SIGINT and aerial refuelling support and US intel assistance. On paper, it’s the most powerful air force in the region after Israel’s.
But despite near-total conventional superiority, Riyadh and its allies have not been able to defeat Ansar Allah, which has no air force, nor stop the targeting of its infrastructure (such attacks have only [intensified](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76159)).
 
🤔Houthis’ hidden hand
 
Just as the US and Israel discovered in Iran, their Saudi counterparts are finding out that air superiority means nothing if you can’t find, target and destroy the enemy’s hard points.
Emerging from the mountainous highlands of Saada, Ansar Allah’s home province provides fighters extensive natural and manmade cover. The region’s jagged limestone and volcanic rock formations are perfect for carving, and extremely dense and durable.
When the Saudis began their air campaign in 2015, the Houthis started engineering large-scale bases and workshops in the mountains, fitting them with thick concrete ceilings, industrial vents, blast doors and safety systems.
Yemen’s experience with fortress building goes back to the 70s, when President Saleh ordered the creation of extensive network of underground strategic command centers and Scud missile bases with East German, Soviet and North Korean engineering help.
When coalition strikes hit these sites, they temporarily block entrances, damage ventilation or cause cosmetic damage, but the bases’ inhabitants and their contents are left unharmed.
The only conceivable way Riyadh could hope to seriously degrade Houthi capabilities in this area would be to use US GBU-57 munitions. But these are only carried by B-2 bombers, and the US has as few as 6 left in its inventory after using 14 in last year’s[ Iran strikes](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/68755).

🇮🇱 Israel on ‘heightened alert’ looking out for Houthi ground, sea assault
 
The IDF is setting up a specialized command hub inside its 80th Edom Territorial Division to prepare for a possible “surprise attack” by Yemen’s Ansar Allah fighters.
Defense officials told JPost the Houthis have ramped up warnings in recent months and weeks about potential “ground attacks” targeting enemies, including Israel, and that their “unpredictability” – which has proven effective against Saudi Arabia, is prompting the IDF to take the threats seriously.
Israeli preparations include setting up a garrison of reserve and rapid-reaction forces around Eilat – Israel’s sole Red Sea port city. The port was previously bankrupted by Ansar Allah after they disrupted Red Sea commercial shipping traffic in [solidarity with Gaza](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/49323).
The deployment will include drills, including with local police and border police forces, an arms buildup, and work to improve coordination and communication between the army, navy and air force.
💬“The Houthis have long since ceased to be regarded as proxies of the Iranians, and they are demonstrating operational independence with an inexplicable determination against the Saudis,” an Israeli defense official admitted, discussing Israel’s preparations.
The potential Yemeni threat is said to feature “prominently in Israeli security assessments.”
It’s not immediately clear what specifically spooked Israel to plan for an all-out Houthi ground or naval assault. The fighters do not possess a conventional blue or even brown water navy, but did recently demonstrate a high level of naval prowess and coordination by rapidly seizing virtually all the islands along the Red Sea coast from the [Saudi-backed](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74365) Aden government.
👉Ansar Allah has spent years asking neighboring nations to give thousands of its fighters safe passage through Saudi Arabia and Jordan to join the fight against Israel. These requests have consistently been [ignored](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/62540).

🇷🇺🧊 Ukraine’s Starlink connection goes haywire amid latest Russian assault
Besides not being warned in advance by NATO ‘partners’ on Russia’s overnight missile strikes in Kiev, Ukrainian forces on the ground have reportedly faced “disrupted frontline operations” after[ new technical restrictions ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76157)were put in place on the use of Elon Musk’s satellite internet service.
Starlink terminals used to operate drones flying 160 km/h+ suffered “signal failures,” disrupting multiple missions Wednesday morning, Ukrainian officials and military personnel told FT.
💬 “Logistics at the frontline and middle strikes are badly limited,” a senior Ukrainian official said. There was “no warning,” with the restrictions just becoming apparent “in the middle of the night,” they said.
[Defense Ministry aide Serhii Beskrestnov said ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75939)it was obvious “this action is not coincidental and is related to the current political situation.”
👉 Musk has not made any formal announcement on the restrictions, but did recently accuse Zelensky of going “too far” by ignoring Trump’s energy ceasefire demands, and saying it’s “time for Ukraine to find a new leader.”
Trump insisted Tuesday that the US continues to do [intel sharing with Ukraine.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76143)
➡️ Musk previously restricted Ukraine’s Starlink access by geofencing coverage to limit Ukrainian strikes deep inside Russia. The US only once briefly paused intel sharing with Ukraine – in March 2025, after an explosive televised Trump-Zelensky exchange at the White House during which Trump accused his counterpart of “gambling with World War Three.”
The immediate chaos at the front once US intel and technological support are put on pause appears to confirm what Russian officials have been saying for almost five years – that this is a NATO proxy war that would end immediately if the West pulled its support for Kiev.
